- When sentiment is positive (≥0.3) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce the peak overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to bullish sentiment.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.2) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — adjust downward only if recent price action confirms trend, otherwise revert to mean.
- For 30-day forecasts, if the last 3–5 days show strong upward momentum, model should not over-forecast beyond +15% above recent high; cap growth to prevent lagged overcorrection.
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating +/–), model should smooth out extreme swings — avoid predicting sharp reversals unless confirmed by price action or macro signals.
- If true outcome exceeds forecast by >10% in 3–5 consecutive days, model should adjust downward in next forecast to avoid mean reversion bias.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if sentiment is consistently positive but price is flat or slightly declining, model should not assume continuation — expect mean reversion or pause in momentum.
- If forecast spikes after a low sentiment period, reduce the magnitude of the spike — sentiment often underestimates recovery speed.
- When sentiment is high but price is stuck near support, model should not assume breakout — wait for confirmation before increasing forecast.
- Avoid forecasting above 10% above recent 18-day high unless sentiment is strongly bullish and confirmed by volume or volatility.
